chapters.title: Meet the Piano Keyboard
chapters.intro: Black and white keys in a row: the piano's secret map!

text: A piano has lots of keys, in two colors: white and black.
White keys are like wide roads, and black keys are like little hills along the road.
Press different keys and you hear sounds that are higher or lower.
pages.tip: A standard piano has 88 keys in all!

text: Look closely: the black keys are not placed at random.
They always squeeze together in a group of two, then a group of three.
Two, then three, like kids lining up.
pages.tip: Count the black keys and you will never get lost!

text: The white key just to the left of the two black keys is C.
The white key just to the left of the three black keys is F.
Finding C and F is like finding landmarks on a map.
pages.tip: C sits right at the front door of the two black keys.

text: The white keys are named with seven letters: C D E F G A B.
They go in order from left to right, and the sound gets higher as you go right.
After B, we come back to C and start over.
pages.tip: The letters stop at G, then start again from A.

pages.h: Middle C and High and Low
text: Near the middle of the keyboard there is a very important C.
It is called "middle C", written C4, and it is our home base for finding notes.
Play to the right and the sound gets higher; play to the left and it gets lower.
pages.tip: Little birds sing high notes on the right; big elephants rumble low notes on the left.

pages.h: The Octave and Names of Black Keys
text: From one C to the next C is called an "octave".
The two notes sound like brothers, one high and one low.
Black keys borrow white-key names: add "sharp" for the right neighbor, "flat" for the left.
pages.tip: The black key to the right of C is called C sharp, and also D flat.

quiz.q: Which note name is the lit-up key?
quiz.e: The white key left of the two black keys is C.

quiz.q: Which note name is the lit-up key?
quiz.e: The white key left of the three black keys is F.

quiz.q: How is middle C written?
quiz.e: Middle C is in the middle of the keyboard and is usually written C4.

quiz.q: How many note names do the white keys use?
quiz.e: The note names are C D E F G A B: seven in all.

quiz.q: When you play to the right of the middle, what happens to the sound?
quiz.e: To the right on the keyboard are high notes, to the left low notes.

quiz.q: What is it called from one C to the next C?
quiz.e: From C to C there are eight white keys, called an octave.

quiz.q: Which note name is the lit-up key?
quiz.e: A is the white key just to the right of the middle one of the three black keys.

quiz.q: Which white key is to the left of the group of three black keys?
quiz.e: Left of the three black keys is F; left of the two black keys is C.

chapters.title: The Staff and Clefs
chapters.intro: A five-story house where the notes live. Let's climb the stairs!

pages.h: The Staff Is Like Five Stairs
text: The staff has five lines. Count from the bottom up: first line, second line ... fifth line.
The empty gaps between the lines are called "spaces". There are four of them.
A note can sit on a line or live in a space.
pages.tip: Lines are like floors, spaces are like rooms, and notes are the residents.

text: A clef is like a house number: it tells us the names of the notes.
The treble clef is also called the G clef, and it circles the second line.
The little curl of the clef circles the line that is G.
pages.tip: When you draw a clef, start curling from the second line.

text: The bass clef is also called the F clef, and it is used to write low notes.
Its two little dots hug the fourth line, and that line is F.
The low notes played by the left hand are often written with it.
pages.tip: The two dots are like the two eyes of the F.

pages.h: The Grand Staff and Middle C
text: The piano is played with two hands, so we join two staves together.
The top one is the treble staff and the bottom one is the bass staff.
Middle C lives in a little room right between the two staves.
pages.tip: Middle C is the "stairwell" between the high floor and the low floor.

text: What if a note is too high or too low to fit on the staff?
We add a short little line above or below, just for that note.
These are called "ledger lines", like building an extra floor on a house.
pages.tip: A ledger line is drawn only next to the note, never all the way across.

text: To read music, look at the clef first, then count lines and spaces from the bottom up.
In the treble clef the lines are E G B D F, and the spaces are F A C E.
Read it a few more times and the notes will start to talk by themselves.
pages.tip: The four spaces together spell the word FACE.

quiz.q: How many lines does the staff have?
quiz.e: A five-line staff, as the name says, has five lines.

quiz.q: What is the note name of this note?
quiz.e: The treble clef circles the second line, and that is G.

quiz.q: What is the note name of this note?
quiz.e: The first line of the treble staff is E.

quiz.q: What is the note name of this note?
quiz.e: The bass clef hugs the fourth line, and that is F.

quiz.q: What is the treble clef also called?
quiz.e: It circles G, so it is called the G clef.

quiz.q: What is this note called?
quiz.e: It sits between the two staves, so it is middle C.

quiz.q: In which direction do we count the lines of the staff?
quiz.e: Lines and spaces are both counted from the bottom up.

quiz.q: What is the note name of this note?
quiz.e: A lives in the second space of the treble staff.

chapters.title: Notes and Rests
chapters.intro: Notes can be long or short, and rests can talk too!

text: A note looks like a little tadpole, with a round head and a thin tail.
The round part is the notehead, the straight part is the stem, and the curly part is the flag.
Different shapes mean different lengths.
pages.tip: Stems point up below the middle line and down above it.

text: The whole note is an empty circle with no stem, and it is the longest.
The half note is empty with a stem; the quarter note is filled in with a stem.
The eighth note has one flag, and the sixteenth note has two flags.
pages.tip: The more flags, the shorter the note, and the faster it runs.

text: A note value is how long you sing or play a note.
If the quarter note gets one beat, a whole note is 4 beats.
Each one is twice the next, like cutting a cake in half again and again.
pages.tip: One whole note equals two half notes.

text: A rest means it is time to be quiet: no sound here.
Silence still has to be counted, like playing the "Freeze" game.
Every kind of note has a matching rest with the same length.
pages.tip: A rest is not a break. It is quietly counting the beats.

text: The little dot to the right of a note is called a dot.
A dot makes the note longer by half of its original value.
Dotted half note: 2 beats plus 1 beat makes 3 beats.
pages.tip: A dot is like giving the note a little extra cookie.

text: In 4/4, each measure has to add up to 4 beats.
A half note plus a quarter note plus another quarter note makes exactly 4 beats.
Treat notes like building blocks and build a measure: that is a rhythm game.
pages.tip: Two eighth notes together make one beat.

quiz.q: What note is this?
quiz.e: A filled-in notehead with a stem and no flag.

quiz.q: If the quarter note gets one beat, how many beats is this note?
quiz.e: The whole note is the longest: 4 beats.

quiz.q: If the quarter note gets one beat, how many beats is this note?
quiz.e: A half note is 2 beats, and the dot adds 1 more beat.

quiz.q: How many quarter notes equal one half note?
quiz.e: A half note is 2 beats and a quarter note is 1 beat.

quiz.q: What rest is this?
quiz.e: It rests for 1 beat.

quiz.q: Two eighth notes together equal what?
quiz.e: Half a beat plus half a beat equals one beat.

quiz.q: What does a dot do?
quiz.a: Adds half of the note's value
quiz.e: A dot adds half of the value of the note before it.

quiz.q: How many beats are there in this measure of 4/4?
quiz.e: The half note is 2 beats, plus two quarter notes at 1 beat each, makes 4 beats.

chapters.title: Beat and Time Signature
chapters.intro: Music has a heartbeat. Count it and you will find it!

text: Put your hand on your chest and you can feel your heart going thump-thump.
Music has a steady heartbeat like that, called the "beat".
Walking and clapping are both ways of keeping the beat.
pages.tip: A heartbeat doesn't go fast and then slow, and the beat doesn't either.

text: Some beats are heavy and some are light, like walking with a heavy left foot and a light right foot.
The heavy one is called the strong beat, and the light one the weak beat.
When strong and weak repeat in a pattern, we get meter.
pages.tip: The first beat is always the strongest one!

text: Music is long, so we divide it into little sections.
Each section is called a "measure", and the vertical line between them is called a bar line.
Every measure has the same number of beats.
pages.tip: Bar lines are like little fences that fence the notes into groups.

text: A time signature is two numbers stacked on top of each other, written after the clef.
The top number tells how many beats are in each measure.
The bottom number tells which note gets one beat: 4 means the quarter note.
pages.tip: 3/4 is read "three-four": three beats in every measure.

text: 2/4 has two beats, like walking: left, right, left, right.
3/4 has three beats, like spinning around in a waltz.
4/4 is the most common, like clapping: strong, weak, medium, weak.
pages.tip: Waltzes go in three; marches go in two or four.

text: 6/8 has six eighth notes in a measure, grouped into two big groups.
Each group has three notes, and it feels like "strong weak weak, medium weak weak".
Conductors draw shapes with their hands to show the beat; here is a common pattern.
pages.tip: The path the baton draws is a map of the beat.

quiz.q: In 3/4, how many beats are in each measure?
quiz.e: The top number 3 means 3 beats in each measure.

quiz.q: In 4/4, what does the bottom 4 mean?
quiz.a: A quarter note gets one beat
w: There are 4 beats in a measure
An eighth note gets one beat
quiz.e: The bottom number tells the unit of the beat.

quiz.q: Which time signature do waltzes usually use?
quiz.e: A waltz has three beats and usually uses 3/4.

quiz.q: What separates one measure from the next?
quiz.e: The vertical line is called a bar line.

quiz.q: What is the strong-weak pattern of four beats?
quiz.e: The first beat is strong and the third beat is medium.

quiz.q: In 6/8, one measure equals how many eighth notes?
quiz.e: The top number is 6, and the bottom 8 means eighth notes.

quiz.q: What is the direction of the conducting pattern for three beats?
quiz.e: The path for three beats is down, right, up.

quiz.q: Into how many groups are the six eighth notes of 6/8 usually divided?
quiz.e: Three notes to a group, two big groups in all.

chapters.title: Rhythm Patterns
chapters.intro: Tie it, join it, hop along: rhythm can be anything!

text: Two notes of the same pitch joined by a curved line make a tie.
Play only the first note and let it keep ringing until the end of the second.
Add up the values: a half note plus a quarter note makes 3 beats.
pages.tip: A tie is like a rubber band that stretches two notes into one.

text: A curved line over notes of different pitches is called a slur.
Play these notes smoothly connected, like singing them in one breath.
Every note is still played, unlike a tie, which merges notes.
pages.tip: Look closely: the same pitch means a tie, different pitches mean a slur.

text: Normally strong beats are heavy and weak beats are light, but syncopation likes to play tricks.
It puts the accent on a weak beat or a weak position.
It sounds a little bouncy, and there is lots of it in jazz.
pages.tip: Syncopation is like stepping off the beat on purpose, and it is even more fun.

text: Usually a beat is split in half, into two eighth notes.
A triplet splits one beat into three equal parts.
On the music it is marked with a little 3, like three kids squeezed into one row.
pages.tip: Two notes in a beat, three notes in a beat: squeeze them in!

text: Some songs don't start on the first beat; they "get a running start" first.
The first measure is incomplete, and it is called a pickup measure.
The last measure is a few beats short, and together the two make one full measure.
pages.tip: A pickup is like a run-up before a jump, a little warm-up.

text: Common rhythm patterns include even notes, dotted rhythms, syncopation and more.
Dotted rhythm: a dotted eighth note plus a sixteenth note, short and punchy.
Remember them, and you can read rhythms quickly when you see the music.
pages.tip: Rhythm patterns are the "everyday words" of rhythm.

quiz.q: What is the curved line that joins two notes of the same pitch called?
quiz.e: Joining the same pitch makes a tie.

quiz.q: Two quarter notes joined together make how many beats in all?
quiz.e: A tie adds the values: 1 plus 1 is 2.

quiz.q: How should a slur be played?
w: Play one note, rest one beat
quiz.e: A slur asks for the notes to be connected smoothly.

quiz.q: Into how many parts does a triplet divide a beat?
quiz.e: A triplet divides one beat evenly into three.

quiz.q: What is special about a pickup measure?
quiz.a: Fewer beats than a full measure
w: More beats than a full measure
quiz.e: A pickup measure is not a full measure.

quiz.q: What is this rhythm called?
quiz.e: The accent falls on a weak position: that is syncopation.

quiz.q: How many beats is a dotted eighth note?
quiz.e: An eighth note is half a beat, plus half of that, makes 3/4 beat.

quiz.q: Where does the accent of a syncopation fall?
quiz.a: On a weak beat or weak position
quiz.e: Move the accent to a weak position and you have syncopation.

chapters.title: Tempo
chapters.intro: Is the music running fast or slow? Let's measure the speed!

text: The same song sung fast or slow feels completely different.
How fast or slow music goes is called the "tempo".
The tempo is usually written at the very top of the first line of the music.
pages.tip: Lullabies are slow and sleepy; playful pieces hop and skip.

text: Classical music often uses Italian words for tempo.
Largo is the slowest and Presto is the fastest, and the rest are in between.
The numbers are about how many beats per minute.
pages.tip: Andante is like a relaxed stroll, and Allegro is like a little jog.

text: BPM is how many beats there are in a minute, written like ♩=60.
60 means 60 beats in a minute, which is one beat every second.
The bigger the number, the closer the beats and the faster the music.
pages.tip: At ♩=120, each beat lasts only half a second.

text: A metronome is a little helper that goes "tick-tock".
Set the BPM and it taps out the beat steadily.
When you practice, start slowly, and speed up little by little once it is easy.
pages.tip: Don't run faster than the metronome. It won't get angry, but you will get mixed up!

text: The tempo sometimes changes, like a roller coaster that goes fast and slow.
rit. means getting slower, like a car slowly braking.
accel. means getting faster, and a tempo means going back to the original speed.
pages.tip: rit. is short for the Italian word ritardando.

quiz.q: What does Allegro mean?
quiz.e: Allegro means fast and cheerful.

quiz.q: Which of these tempos is the slowest?
quiz.e: Largo is the broadest and slowest.

quiz.q: At ♩=60, how long is each beat?
quiz.e: 60 beats in a minute is exactly one beat per second.

quiz.q: At ♩=120, how long is each beat?
quiz.e: 120 beats in a minute is half a second per beat.

quiz.q: What does this mark mean?
quiz.e: rit. means getting slower.

quiz.q: What does this mark mean?
quiz.e: accel. means getting faster.

quiz.q: Which of these tempos is faster than Andante?
quiz.e: Moderato is moderate, faster than Andante.

quiz.q: What does a metronome do?
quiz.e: A metronome helps us keep a steady tempo.

chapters.title: Dynamics and Expression
chapters.intro: Music breathes: sometimes loud, sometimes soft, sometimes short, sometimes smooth!

text: Say the same sentence quietly and it's a whisper. Say it loudly and it's a shout.
Music works the same way. How loud or soft a sound is is called "dynamics".
Composers mark dynamics with abbreviations of Italian words, and pianists all over the world can read them.
p means soft, f means loud. Remember: p is like setting something down gently, f is like clapping hard.
pages.tip: p = piano (soft), f = forte (loud).

text: pp is softer than p, ff is louder than f. Each extra letter adds one more level.
m means "medium". mp is on the p side, mf is on the f side.
From softest to loudest, line them up: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff.
Your fingers press with different strength, so the sound changes. Listen with your ears!

fig.s: pp < p < mp < mf < f < ff

pages.tip: The m in mp and mf both mean "medium".

text: The sound can slowly grow bigger, like a balloon being blown up. This is called "crescendo".
The sound can also slowly fade, like a car driving away. This is called "decrescendo" or "diminuendo".
Crescendo is written cresc. or drawn as an opening "＜".
Decrescendo is written dim. or decresc., or drawn as a closing "＞".
pages.tip: A mouth opening wider and wider = crescendo.

text: A little dot above or below a note head means "staccato". Play it short and bouncy, like a little bunny hopping.
When there is no gap between the notes and they flow like singing, it is called "legato".
Legato is often shown by a curved line, the "slur", joining the notes: one breath, played like one sentence.
With no marks at all, play in the normal way: not joined, not too detached.
pages.tip: Staccato is like a dragonfly touching the water, legato is like rowing a boat.

text: A "＞" above a note is called an "accent". That note should stand out.
It's like stressing a word when you speak: "I—want—an—APPLE!"
A small dot under a curved arc above a note is called a "fermata".
When you see it, you may hold the note longer. The player decides how long, usually about twice as long.
pages.tip: A fermata is like pressing the "pause button" on a note.

quiz.q: How do you say this mark?
quiz.e: ff means very loud.

quiz.q: Which mark means "soft"?
quiz.e: p is piano, which means soft.

quiz.q: What does mf mean?
quiz.e: m is medium and f is loud, so together: medium loud.

quiz.q: Which sound is the softest?
quiz.e: pp is very soft, even quieter than p.

quiz.q: What does the "crescendo" sign look like?
quiz.e: The ＜ opens wider and wider, and the sound gets louder and louder.

quiz.q: What does a small dot on a note head mean?
quiz.e: A dot means staccato: short and bouncy.

quiz.q: What is the "＞" on a note called?
quiz.e: ＞ is an accent: make this note stand out.

quiz.q: What should you do when you see a fermata?
quiz.e: A fermata lets the note stay a little longer.

chapters.title: Sharps, Flats and Naturals
chapters.intro: Black keys have names. Sharp, flat and natural, the three brothers, come to help!

text: Two keys right next to each other on the piano are the closest possible distance. This is called a "half step".
Two notes with one key between them are two half steps apart. This is called a "whole step".
E to F is a half step because there is no black key between them.
C to D is a whole step because a black key sits in between.
pages.tip: There is no black key between white keys E-F and B-C.

text: The sharp is written "♯" and raises a note by one half step.
On the piano, you move one key to the right, whether it is black or white.
F raised by a half step is F♯, the black key just right of F.
Remember: a sharp is like a bird flying up, so the sound gets higher.
pages.tip: The arrows in ♯ all point up, so it means higher.

text: The flat is written "♭" and lowers a note by one half step, which means one key to the left.
B lowered by a half step is B♭, the black key just left of B.
The natural is written "♮" and cancels an earlier sharp or flat, going back to the original note.
A sharp or flat lasts for the rest of the measure, and stops at the bar line.
pages.tip: A natural sign is like the "undo button".

text: One black key can have two names: C♯ is also called D♭.
They are played on the same key and sound exactly the same. This is called "enharmonic".
It's like a person with a real name and a nickname: whichever you call, it's the same person.
Which name to use depends on the key of the piece.
pages.tip: F♯ and G♭ are also a pair.

text: The black keys come in groups of two and three, like two little birds and three little birds.
The two black keys: C♯ (D♭) and D♯ (E♭).
The three black keys: F♯ (G♭), G♯ (A♭) and A♯ (B♭).
To find C, first find a group of two black keys. The white key just to their left is C.
pages.tip: Left of the two black keys is C, left of the three black keys is F.

quiz.q: What is "♯" called?
quiz.e: ♯ is a sharp, which raises a note by a half step.

quiz.q: What does the flat "♭" do?
quiz.e: ♭ lowers a note by one half step.

quiz.q: Which two keys are a half step apart?
quiz.e: There is no black key between E and F, so it is a half step.

quiz.q: What is the distance from C to D?
quiz.e: C and D have C♯ between them: two half steps, which is a whole step.

quiz.q: What does the natural "♮" do?
quiz.e: ♮ cancels an earlier sharp or flat.

quiz.q: What is the enharmonic name of C♯?
quiz.e: C♯ and D♭ are the same black key.

quiz.q: What is F raised by a half step?
quiz.e: One key right of F is F♯.

quiz.q: What is the leftmost key of the group of three black keys called?
quiz.e: The group of three starts with F♯.

chapters.title: Major Scales
chapters.intro: A scale is a musical ladder: climb it one step at a time.

text: A scale is a "staircase" made by arranging notes from low to high, one step at a time.
The most common one is the major scale. It has 7 different notes, and the 8th goes back to the start.
The steps follow a pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
Follow this pattern from any note and you can climb a major scale.
pages.tip: Memory trick: two wholes, a half; three wholes, a half.

text: Starting on C, all white keys and no black keys: this is C major.
C D E F G A B C. E-F and B-C happen to be half steps, exactly as the pattern says.
So C major needs no sharps and no flats.
When learning scales, starting with this one is the easiest.
pages.tip: C major is the "white-key scale".

text: Every note in the scale has a solfège name: do re mi fa sol la si do.
You can also call them by numbers: 1st degree, 2nd degree ... 7th degree.
The 1st degree is the most important. It is called the "tonic", the home of the scale.
The 5th degree is called the "dominant" and the 4th is the "subdominant". They are good neighbors of home.
pages.tip: Solfège do re mi are the nicknames of the scale.

text: Starting on G, climb the stairs with "whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half".
G-A whole, A-B whole, B-C half, C-D whole, D-E whole, E-F♯ whole, F♯-G half.
Notice the 7th note must be F♯, not F, otherwise it wouldn't be a whole step.
So G major has one sharp: F♯.
pages.tip: The only black key in G major is F♯.

text: F major starts on F: F G A B♭ C D E F.
The 4th note must be lowered to B♭, so that A-B♭ is a whole step and B♭-C is a whole step.
D major starts on D: D E F♯ G A B C♯ D, with two sharps.
Every major scale uses the same formula, only the starting note and the sharps or flats differ.
pages.tip: F major has one flat: B♭.

quiz.q: What is the step pattern of a major scale?
quiz.e: A major scale is whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half.

quiz.q: How many different notes does a major scale have?
quiz.e: A major scale has 7 different notes.

quiz.q: How many sharps or flats are in C major?
quiz.e: C major is all white keys.

quiz.q: Which scale degree is solfège sol?
quiz.e: do re mi fa sol: sol is the 5th degree.

quiz.q: What is the 1st degree of a scale called?
quiz.e: The 1st degree is the tonic, the home of the scale.

quiz.q: Which major scale is this?
quiz.e: It starts on G and contains F♯.

quiz.q: Which note is lowered in F major?
quiz.e: F major has one flat, B♭.

quiz.q: How many sharps does D major have?
quiz.e: D major has F♯ and C♯, so 2 sharps.

chapters.title: Key Signatures and the Circle of Fifths
chapters.intro: The key signature is a piece's ID card, and the circle of fifths is its map!

text: A piece has lots of F♯s. Writing a ♯ every single time would be so tiring!
So composers gather the sharps or flats right after the clef. This is called the "key signature".
The key signature rules the whole piece: every note it names must be raised or lowered.
With a key signature, the music looks clean and tidy.
pages.tip: A key signature is like a class rule: everyone must follow it.

text: Sharps always appear in a fixed order: F C G D A E B.
One sharp is G major, two sharps is D major, and so on.
C major has no sharps and is the starting point.
Memory trick: the sharp keys in order are C G D A E B F♯, one more sharp each time.
pages.tip: Each extra sharp moves the tonic up a perfect fifth.

text: Flats appear in the reverse order: B E A D G C F.
F major has one flat, B♭. B♭ major has two: B♭ and E♭.
The flat keys in order are C F B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭, one more flat each time.
The order of flats is exactly the order of sharps read backwards.
pages.tip: Sharps: FCGDAEB. Flats: BEADGCF.

text: Put all the keys around a circle like a clock face. This is the "circle of fifths".
C major is at the top. Each step clockwise adds one sharp.
Each step counterclockwise adds one flat.
At the bottom the sharp keys and flat keys meet. For example, F♯ and G♭ are enharmonic.
pages.tip: Neighboring keys on the circle differ by only one sharp or flat.

pages.h: How to Find the Key of a Piece
text: First look at the key signature: how many sharps or flats are there?
Sharp keys: go one half step up from the last sharp, and that is the tonic.
Example: two sharps F♯ C♯. The last is C♯, a half step above is D, so it is D major.
Flat keys: the second-to-last flat is the tonic. With only one flat, it is F major.
Finally, look at the last note of the piece. It is usually the tonic and can help you check.
pages.tip: For sharp keys: "last sharp, go up a half step".

quiz.q: Where is the key signature written?
w: At the end of the piece
quiz.e: The key signature is written after the clef.

quiz.q: What is the order of sharps?
quiz.e: The order of sharps is always FCGDAEB.

quiz.q: How many sharps does G major have?
quiz.e: G major has only F♯.

quiz.q: What is the order of flats?
quiz.e: The order of flats is the reverse of the order of sharps.

quiz.q: How many flats does F major have?
quiz.e: F major has only B♭.

quiz.q: Two sharps (F♯ C♯): which key is it?
quiz.e: A half step above the last sharp, C♯, is D.

quiz.q: Which key is at the top of the circle of fifths?
quiz.e: The circle of fifths starts at C major.

quiz.q: Going one step clockwise, what happens to the sharps?
quiz.e: Each step clockwise adds one sharp.

chapters.title: Minor Scales
chapters.intro: Major is like a sunny day, minor is like a moonlit night. Each has its own beauty.

text: Major sounds bright and cheerful, like a sunny day.
Minor sounds soft and a little sad, like a story told by moonlight.
The most basic minor scale is the "natural minor". Its steps are: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole.
Starting on A, all white keys: that is A natural minor.
pages.tip: A minor is the "white-key minor", the partner of C major.

text: The 7th note of natural minor is a whole step from the tonic, which doesn't sound "tight" enough.
Raise the 7th note by a half step and it becomes the "harmonic minor".
A harmonic minor: A B C D E F G♯ A.
It has an exotic, Eastern flavor. Between F and G♯ there are three half steps, like one big stride.
pages.tip: Harmonic minor: raise the 7th note.

text: To make it sing smoothly, the melodic minor raises both the 6th and 7th notes by a half step going up.
A melodic minor going up: A B C D E F♯ G♯ A.
Going down, it goes back to natural minor: A G F E D C B A.
Remember: going up, raise two; going down, raise none.
pages.tip: Melodic minor: "changes going up, no changes going down".

text: There is a pair of good friends that share the same key signature but have different tonics. They are called "relative major and minor".
Count down three half steps (a minor third) from the major tonic and you reach its relative minor.
The relative minor of C major is A minor, of G major is E minor, of F major is D minor.
Their key signatures are exactly the same.
pages.tip: The tonic of the relative minor is the 6th degree of the major scale.

pages.h: Parallel Keys and Common Minor Keys
text: A major key and a minor key with the same tonic are called "parallel keys", such as C major and C minor.
They are like twins: same name, different temper, and different key signatures.
E minor has one sharp, F♯. D minor has one flat, B♭.
A minor has no sharps or flats.
pages.tip: E minor has the same key signature as G major.

quiz.q: How many sharps or flats does A natural minor have?
quiz.e: A minor is all white keys.

quiz.q: What is the step pattern of natural minor?
quiz.e: Natural minor: whole-half-whole-whole-half-whole-whole.

quiz.q: Which note does harmonic minor raise?
quiz.e: Harmonic minor raises the 7th note.

quiz.q: Which sharp appears in A harmonic minor?
quiz.e: A harmonic minor has G♯.

quiz.q: Which two notes does melodic minor raise going up?
quiz.e: Going up, the 6th and 7th notes are raised.

quiz.q: What is the relative minor of C major?
quiz.e: C major pairs with A minor.

quiz.q: What is the relative minor of G major?
quiz.e: The relative minor of G major is E minor.

quiz.q: What do a major key and a minor key with the same tonic form?
quiz.e: For example, C major and C minor are parallel keys.

chapters.title: Intervals
chapters.intro: The distance between two notes is measured in "numbers"!

text: An interval is the distance between two notes, like measuring how far apart two trees are.
Two notes sounding together form a "harmonic interval", like two people talking at once.
Notes sounding one after the other form a "melodic interval", like singing.
The size of an interval is counted in "numbers".
pages.tip: Together is harmonic, one after the other is melodic.

text: To count an interval, the starting note is 1. Count up one by one until you reach the top note.
C to E: C is 1, D is 2, E is 3, so it is a 3rd.
C to G: C D E F G, you counted 5 notes, so it is a 5th.
Counting the same note once gives a 1st, called a unison.
pages.tip: When counting, include both the first and the last note.

text: The number is not enough. You also need the "quality": perfect, major, minor, augmented or diminished.
1sts, 4ths, 5ths and 8ths can only be "perfect". 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths can be "major" or "minor".
A major interval is one half step bigger than a minor interval.
A half step bigger than major or perfect is "augmented", a half step smaller than minor or perfect is "diminished".
pages.tip: The number of half steps is the number of keys, black and white both count.

text: Some intervals sound very harmonious when played together. They are called "consonant intervals".
The perfect unison and perfect octave are the most consonant, and perfect 4ths and 5ths are also very stable.
Major and minor 3rds and 6ths sound sweet and are also consonant.
2nds, 7ths and augmented or diminished intervals sound tense. They are called "dissonant intervals".
Dissonant doesn't mean ugly. It gives music tension, like a little trouble in a story.
pages.tip: Dissonance is the "seasoning" of music.

text: Moving the lower note of an interval up an octave is called "inversion".
C-E (a 3rd) inverted becomes E-C (a 6th). The two numbers add up to 9.
The quality changes too: major becomes minor, minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, diminished becomes augmented, and perfect stays perfect.
For example, a major 3rd inverts to a minor 6th, and a perfect 5th inverts to a perfect 4th.
pages.tip: The numbers add up to 9, and major and minor swap.

quiz.q: What number interval is C to E?
quiz.e: C D E is 3 notes, so it is a 3rd.

quiz.q: What number interval is C to G?
quiz.e: C D E F G is 5 notes, so it is a 5th.

quiz.q: When counting an interval, what number is the starting note?
quiz.e: The starting note counts, and you begin counting from 1.

quiz.q: How many half steps are in a perfect 5th?
quiz.e: A perfect 5th is 7 half steps.

quiz.q: How many half steps are in a major 3rd?
quiz.e: A major 3rd has 4 half steps, a minor 3rd has 3.

quiz.q: Which interval is the most consonant?
quiz.e: The perfect unison and perfect octave are the most consonant.

quiz.q: Which of these is a dissonant interval?
quiz.e: 2nds and 7ths are dissonant intervals.

quiz.q: What does a perfect 5th become when inverted?
quiz.e: 5 plus 4 equals 9, and a perfect interval stays perfect when inverted.

chapters.title: Chords
chapters.intro: Stack three notes together and you build a little house of music!

pages.h: Chords are building blocks of sound
text: One note is like one building block. Stack three and you have a chord.
The most common chord is the triad: skip a note, then stack a block.
Start on C: C, skip D, stack E, skip F, then stack G.
Play C, E and G together and it sounds bright and steady.
pages.tip: Three notes sounding together make a chord.

text: The three blocks in a triad each have a name.
The bottom one is the root. Like the root of a tree, it gives the chord its name.
The middle one is the third. It decides whether the chord sounds bright or sad.
The top one is the fifth, because it is five letter names away from the root.
pages.tip: Root at the bottom, third in the middle, fifth on top.

text: Triads come in four personalities, decided by the size of two "stairs".
A major third is 4 half steps, a minor third is 3 half steps.
Major triad: major third plus minor third. Cheerful.
Minor triad: minor third plus major third. Gentle and a bit sad.
An augmented triad has two major thirds, a diminished triad has two minor thirds.
pages.tip: A major chord is like a sunny day, a minor chord like a cloudy day.

pages.h: Inversions: a new way to stand
text: The notes of a chord can change order, like three classmates swapping places.
Root at the bottom is called root position: C E G.
Move the root to the top, so the third is lowest: first inversion, E G C.
Now move the third up too, so the fifth is lowest: second inversion, G C E.
The note names stay the same, only the lowest note changes, and the sound feels lighter.
pages.tip: Look at the lowest note to know which inversion it is.

text: Sheet music often uses letters to tell you which chord to play.
C is a C major triad, Cm is minor, Caug or C+ is augmented.
Cdim or C° is a diminished triad.
C/E is read "C over E" and means: play E as the lowest note.
In a major key we also use Roman numerals: I is the first-degree chord, V is the fifth-degree chord.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: C chord with E as the lowest note

pages.tip: The letter after the slash is the lowest note.

quiz.q: What chord is this?
quiz.e: C, E, G: a major third from C up to E, then a minor third up to G.

quiz.q: What is the most common way to stack a triad?
quiz.e: Stacking in thirds: every block skips one note.

quiz.q: Which key is the third of the C chord?
quiz.e: C is the root, E is the third, G is the fifth.

quiz.q: Which two thirds make a major triad?
quiz.e: A major third on the bottom, a minor third on top.

quiz.q: What chord is C E G#?
quiz.e: C to E and E to G# are both major thirds.

quiz.q: Which position of the C chord is this?
quiz.e: The lowest note is the third, E, so it is first inversion.

quiz.q: Which three notes make an Am chord?
quiz.e: Minor triad: A, then a minor third up to C, then a major third up to E.

quiz.q: What does G/B mean?
quiz.a: A G chord with B as the lowest note
w: A B chord with G as the lowest note
quiz.e: The letter after the slash is the lowest note. Here it is a first inversion.

chapters.title: Seventh Chords and Extensions
chapters.intro: Add one more layer on top of a triad and the building gets taller!

text: Stack one more block, skipping a note, on top of a triad and you get a seventh chord.
The top note is a seventh away from the root, so it is called the seventh.
C E G plus B makes C E G B.
A chord with four notes sounds richer and a bit more jazzy.
pages.tip: A seventh chord has four notes, a triad only three.

text: Major seventh: major triad plus a major seventh. Dreamy and warm.
Minor seventh: minor triad plus a minor seventh. Soft and relaxed.
Dominant seventh: major triad plus a minor seventh. A little tense, it wants to move on.
Diminished seventh: all three layers are minor thirds. Mysterious, like a thriller.
The top note of a diminished seventh is spelled Bbb (B double-flat), but you play it as A.
pages.tip: The 7 in C7 is a minor seventh, not a major seventh.

pages.h: The dominant seventh wants to go home
text: G7 is G B D F, built on the dominant note, G.
The B and F inside it are very unstable, as if shouting "take me home!"
It loves to go to the C chord: B moves up to C, F moves down to E.
Listen: G7 then C. Doesn't it feel like "finally home"?
pages.tip: Dominant seventh to tonic chord is music's favorite road home.

text: sus means suspended: the third is "hung up" and left out.
sus4: use the fourth, F, instead of the third, E, to get C F G.
sus2: use the second, D, instead of the third to get C D G.
It sounds neither bright nor sad, like hanging in mid-air, waiting to land.
It often resolves to the original major chord.
pages.tip: A suspended chord is like standing on tiptoe, about to land.

text: In pop music, C6 is C E G plus the sixth, A.
It sounds sweeter than a plain major triad and is often used to end songs.
Careful: in textbooks, a "six chord" often means the first inversion of a triad.
That is because from root position to first inversion, the lowest note and the root are a sixth apart.
So check the context: in pop charts read the letters, in textbooks read the inversion.
pages.tip: In letter symbols, C6 is a chord with one extra note.

text: Left hand plays the root, right hand plays the whole chord: the simplest accompaniment.
Press the three notes of the right hand at the same moment, like little birds landing together.
You can also play them one by one: C, E, G, E, like a flowing stream.
When there are many chords, pick nearby inversions so your hand does not leap.
First play slowly and correctly, then make it sound beautiful.
pages.tip: Notes together make a block chord, one by one make a broken chord.

quiz.q: How many notes does a seventh chord have?
quiz.e: A triad plus one more seventh note makes four.

quiz.q: What seventh chord is this?
quiz.e: C E G B: a major triad plus the major seventh, B.

quiz.q: Which chord does G7 love to go to?
quiz.e: The dominant seventh wants to return to the tonic chord, C.

quiz.q: Which extra note does C7 have compared with a C major triad?
quiz.e: A dominant seventh adds a minor seventh note, Bb.

quiz.q: Which notes make up Csus4?
quiz.e: sus4 uses the fourth, F, instead of the third.

quiz.q: What does sus mean?
quiz.a: Replace the third with a neighboring note
quiz.e: The third is hung up and replaced by the second or the fourth.

quiz.q: Which notes make up Cm7?
quiz.e: A minor triad plus a minor seventh.

quiz.q: Which notes make up the C6 chord?
quiz.e: A major triad plus the sixth, A.

chapters.title: Chord Progressions
chapters.intro: Chords follow one another like a little train rolling into the distance.

text: Build a triad on every note of a major scale and you get seven chords.
In C major: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, Bdim.
Capital Roman numerals I IV V are major triads, lowercase ii iii vi are minor.
The three most important major chords are I, IV and V, the primary triads.
Learn these three and you can accompany lots of songs.
pages.tip: I IV V are the three musketeers of accompaniment.

text: Chords are like classmates in a class, each with a job.
T is the tonic function, degree I. It is "home" and the most stable.
S is the subdominant function, degree IV. It means "going out", leaving home.
D is the dominant function, degree V. It is "on the way home" and wants to return most.
A typical journey: T leaves, S goes far, D turns back, T arrives home.
pages.tip: T-S-D-T is the most basic story in harmony.

pages.h: Cadences: the full stops of a phrase
text: A cadence is the chord ending a phrase, like punctuation in a sentence.
Authentic cadence V→I: like a full stop, very complete.
Plagal cadence IV→I: like singing "Amen", soft and calm.
Half cadence stops on V: like a comma, the sentence is not finished.
Deceptive cadence V→vi: like "Oh, not home yet!", a pleasant surprise.
pages.tip: V→I is a full stop, stopping on V is a comma.

text: The Canon progression comes from the Baroque "Canon in D".
In C major it is C, G, Am, Em, F, C, F, G.
In numerals: I V vi iii IV I IV V.
Eight chords, with the bass walking down step by step like going downstairs.
Many pop songs borrow it, and it sounds especially warm.
pages.tip: The bass of the Canon progression walks down like stairs.

text: The favorite of pop songs is I V vi IV, called 1564.
The numbers 1, 5, 6, 4 are degrees of the scale.
In C major that is C, G, Am, F.
Put different melodies on the same chords and you can write hundreds of songs.
To change key, just change the root. The pattern stays the same.
pages.tip: 1564 is like a magic formula that songs love to use.

quiz.q: Which notes make up the I chord in C major?
quiz.e: The I chord is built on the tonic, C.

quiz.q: In C major, which degree is this chord?
quiz.e: G B D is built on the fifth note, G.

quiz.q: What is the IV chord in G major?
quiz.e: The fourth note of G major is C, so the chord is C E G.

quiz.q: Which degree's chord matches the dominant function, D?
quiz.e: The dominant function is represented by the V chord.

quiz.q: Which two chords make an authentic cadence?
quiz.e: Dominant to tonic is the most complete full stop.

quiz.q: What is the IV → I cadence called?
quiz.e: Subdominant to tonic, also called the "Amen cadence".

quiz.q: What is the 1564 progression in C major?
Which chord does a half cadence stop on?
quiz.e: Stopping on V is like a comma.

chapters.title: Piano Playing Basics
chapters.intro: Sit well, place your hands well, and your little hands can play beautiful sounds!

text: Sit on the front half of the bench, back straight, not leaning on the backrest.
Face the middle of the piano, with your elbows about as high as the keys.
Relax your hand like you are gently holding a small ball, fingers naturally curved.
Do not let your wrist sink, and do not lift it too high.
Relax your shoulders, do not hunch them, and do not hold your breath.
pages.tip: Imagine holding a little egg in your palm.

text: Each finger of each hand has a number, starting with the thumb.
1 is the thumb, 2 is the index finger, 3 is the middle finger.
4 is the ring finger, 5 is the pinky.
Left and right hand use the same numbers, the thumb is always 1.
The small numbers beside notes in the score tell you which finger to use.
pages.tip: The thumb is the shortest and most flexible, the team captain number 1.

text: Right hand on C D E F G: finger 1 on C, 2 on D, 3 on E, 4 on F, 5 on G.
Left hand on C3 to G3: finger 5 on C, 4 on D, 3 on E, 2 on F, 1 on G.
For a scale longer than five notes, the thumb tucks under.
C major, right hand: 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5.
Left hand: 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1.
pages.tip: When the thumb tucks under, keep your wrist relaxed.

text: The piano has pedals under it that you control with your foot.
The right one is the sustain pedal. Press it and the sound lasts longer, like an echo.
The left one is the soft pedal. Press it and the sound becomes quieter and softer.
The middle one on a grand piano is the sostenuto pedal.
When changing chords, lift the pedal and press again, or the sounds will blur together.
pages.tip: Keep your heel on the floor and move only your toes on the pedal.

text: The same key can sound completely different depending on how you press it.
Legato: one note flows into the next, like walking hand in hand.
Staccato: short and bouncy, like a ball bouncing again and again.
Press with the pads of your fingers and use the weight of your arm.
Imagine the sound you want first, then press the key, and the sound will obey you.
pages.tip: Smooth and connected is legato, short and detached is staccato.

text: The secret to playing well is not more, but correct.
Split a piece into small sections and practice one small section at a time.
Play slowly first, hands separately, then put them together.
Use a metronome, from slow to fast, only a little faster each time.
A little every day is more useful than one long session a week.
pages.tip: Slow is the fastest way to practice.

quiz.q: Which finger number is the thumb?
quiz.e: On each hand the thumb is finger 1.

quiz.q: In the right-hand C position, which finger plays C4?
quiz.e: In the right-hand C position, finger 1 plays C.

quiz.q: What is the fingering for the C major scale going up, right hand?
quiz.e: After E, the thumb tucks under to the F position.

quiz.q: What is the right pedal of the piano called?
quiz.e: Pressing it makes the sound last longer.

quiz.q: What should your hand shape look like when playing?
w: Fingers sticking up like chicken claws
quiz.e: Fingers naturally curved, hand relaxed.

quiz.q: When learning a new piece, what is the best first step?
w: Play the whole piece fast right away
quiz.e: Slow, hands separate, is how you play accurately.

quiz.q: What does staccato feel like?
quiz.e: Staccato should be short and light.

quiz.q: How should you sit on the piano bench?
quiz.e: Sit on the front half so your arms can move freely.

chapters.title: Musical Form
chapters.intro: A piece of music is like a map, with a start, some turns and a destination.

text: Speech comes in sentences, and music has phrases.
A phrase is like a sentence sung in one breath, often 4 measures long.
Two phrases together often form a period, often 8 measures.
The first phrase is like a question and the second like the answer.
Where you hear the music "breathe" is the end of a phrase.
pages.tip: A phrase is one sentence of music.

text: So they do not have to write things out twice, composers invented repeat signs.
Two thin lines with dots: repeat from the start sign to the end sign.
Sometimes there are 1st and 2nd endings: the second time, skip 1. and play 2.
D.C. means go back to the beginning, D.S. means go back to the % sign.
Fine means the end, Coda means the ending section, often with "jump to Coda".
pages.tip: D.C. al Fine: go back to the beginning and stop at Fine.

text: We label the sections of a piece with letters: A, B, C.
Binary form is A B: two different parts.
Ternary form is A B A: it comes back to the start, like coming home.
The B in the middle is usually different from A, like a story of a trip.
Many children's songs and short pieces are in ternary form.
pages.tip: ABA: the opening theme comes back at the end.

text: Theme and variations: first you hear a theme, then it is changed in many ways.
The notes can get faster or more decorated, or turn from major to minor.
Mozart wrote twelve variations on "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star".
Each variation is like giving the theme a new outfit.
The "skeleton" of the theme stays the same, so you can still recognize it.
pages.tip: Theme A, variations A1, A2...

pages.h: A first look at sonata form
text: Sonata form is the most important large structure in classical music.
Part one is the exposition: two themes make their entrance.
Part two is the development: the themes are taken apart, changed and sent on adventures.
Part three is the recapitulation: the themes return and the key comes home.
It is often found in the first movement of sonatas and symphonies.
pages.tip: Exposition, development, recapitulation, like a hero's story.

quiz.q: What is this sign?
quiz.e: Two lines with dots make a repeat sign.

quiz.q: What does D.C. mean?
quiz.e: D.C. is Da Capo, meaning back to the beginning.

quiz.q: What does D.S. mean?
quiz.e: D.S. is Dal Segno, back to the sign.

quiz.q: What does Fine mean?
quiz.e: Fine means "the end", the piece finishes here.

quiz.q: What is the structure of ternary form?
quiz.e: The third section returns to the first.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of sonata form?
quiz.e: Exposition, development and recapitulation.

quiz.q: What is typical of theme and variations?
quiz.a: One theme changed again and again
quiz.e: First there is a theme, then it gets dressed up.

quiz.q: How many measures does a phrase often have?
quiz.e: 4 measures is the most common, like one sentence.

chapters.title: Instruments and Music History
chapters.intro: Take a time trip with the orchestra and the great composers!

pages.h: The four groups of the orchestra
text: A symphony orchestra is like a big family split into four groups.
Strings: violin, viola, cello, double bass. They have the most players.
Woodwinds: flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon. Their sound is smooth and round.
Brass: trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba. Their sound is loud and bright.
Percussion: timpani, bass drum, cymbals, triangle. They bring rhythm and color.
pages.tip: The flute is made of metal but belongs to the woodwinds.

text: When you press a piano key, a hammer strikes the strings to make the sound.
So it is a bit like a string instrument and a bit like a percussion instrument.
A piano has 88 keys, from the lowest A0 to the highest C8.
It can play melody and accompaniment at once, so it is called the "king of instruments".
The piano's original name was "pianoforte", meaning "soft-loud", because it can play very softly and very loudly.
pages.tip: One piano is a whole little orchestra.

text: The Baroque period is about 1600 to 1750: the music is splendid and full of ornaments.
Bach was a Baroque master and wrote The Well-Tempered Clavier.
The Classical period is about 1750 to 1820: the music is clear, balanced and graceful.
Mozart was a child prodigy and began composing at age five.
Beethoven used music to express strong feelings and is called a giant of music.
pages.tip: In German, Bach means "brook".

text: The Romantic period is about 1820 to 1900: full of feeling and imagination.
Chopin wrote almost only piano music in his life and is called the "poet of the piano".
Liszt had amazing technique and is the "king of the piano".
Schubert wrote hundreds of art songs.
Tchaikovsky wrote Swan Lake, with both ballet and orchestral music.
pages.tip: Romantic music is like telling secrets from the heart.

text: Impressionism is about 1890 to 1920, like a painter painting blurry light and shadow.
Debussy is the best-known one, and his Clair de lune is like a lake under moonlight.
Ravel was also an Impressionist and wrote Jeux d'eau (Fountains).
The 20th century is modern music, where every new method was tried.
Stravinsky and Bartók are both great masters of modern music.
pages.tip: Impressionism does not draw clear lines, it paints light and color.

text: Learning music means training your eyes, ears and hands together.
Reading: first look at the key signature and time signature, then find familiar patterns.
Listening: first hear high or low, then whether it goes up or down.
Try listening to one chord every day and say whether it is major or minor.
Listen to many famous pieces and connect their names with their melodies.
pages.tip: The more you train your ears, the sharper they get, like a little radar.

quiz.q: Which group of instruments does the trumpet belong to?
quiz.e: Trumpet, horn, trombone and tuba are brass.

quiz.q: Which period does Mozart belong to?
quiz.e: Mozart is a master of the Classical period.

quiz.q: How does a piano make its sound?
quiz.e: The key moves a hammer that strikes the strings.

quiz.q: How many keys does a standard piano have?
quiz.e: 52 white keys plus 36 black keys.

quiz.q: Which period does Bach belong to?
quiz.e: Bach is a master of the Baroque period.

quiz.q: Who is called the "poet of the piano"?
quiz.e: Chopin wrote mainly piano music all his life.

quiz.q: Who is a famous Impressionist composer?
quiz.e: Debussy wrote Clair de lune.

quiz.q: Which instrument is NOT in the string group?
quiz.e: The trombone is a brass instrument.
